title: Energy Time-Series Imputation with Differentially Private Diffusion Models via Clipping-Aware Objective Conditioning

paper.title: Energy Time-Series Imputation with Differentially Private Diffusion Models via Clipping-Aware Objective Conditioning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reliable recovery of missing measurements is important for monitoring and
analysis in energy time-series systems, where fine-grained measurements may
contain sensitive temporal information. Diffusion models trained with
differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) provide a
promising framework for privacy-sensitive energy time-series imputation.
Under cosine diffusion schedules, late timesteps correspond to low
signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where standard ε \varepsilon -prediction
can induce large pre-clipping gradients. Such gradients are more likely to be
clipped, reducing the retained optimization signal.
The artificial intelligence (AI) contribution lies in formulating this
objective–clipping interaction as an objective optimization problem under
fixed-threshold DP-SGD and developing timestep-aware objective conditioning
for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation. The method adopts v v -prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, uses static
loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and introduces
diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before
clipping. For the engineering application, we evaluate the method on five real-world
energy time-series datasets across random point missingness, contiguous block
missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities. Under
matched DP-SGD settings, the proposed method consistently improves
imputation utility over the ε \varepsilon -prediction baseline. Gradient
diagnostics reveal lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced
clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps,
supporting the effectiveness of clipping-aware objective conditioning for
energy time-series imputation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Time-series data in energy monitoring systems often contain missing observations because of sensor faults, communication interruptions, device malfunctions, and signal transmission problems ( Lotfipoor et al., 2023 ) . In applications such as transformer monitoring, smart metering, electricity-load monitoring, and building energy management, imputation is needed to recover missing measurements, while the underlying temporal records may contain sensitive personal or operational information. In particular, fine-grained household electricity-consumption profiles can reveal household activities and occupancy patterns ( Molina-Markham et al., 2010 ; Razavi et al., 2019 ) . Differential privacy therefore provides a principled training framework for energy time-series imputation involving sensitive measurements ( Dwork and Roth, 2014 ; Mao et al., 2024 ) . Diffusion models are particularly well suited to this task because they learn conditional denoising processes for reconstructing missing values ( Tashiro et al., 2021 ; Alcaraz and Strodthoff, 2022 ; Cao et al., 2024 ) . However, under differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD), the denoising objective directly interacts with fixed-threshold gradient clipping. When the objective induces large per-example gradients, clipping attenuates their contributions to the optimization update and can degrade training utility ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) . We identify an objective–clipping interaction that becomes pronounced at late diffusion timesteps, where diffusion timesteps are distinct from training iterations. Under cosine schedules, late diffusion timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ) . In this regime, standard ε \varepsilon -prediction can induce large pre-clipping gradients that exceed the fixed clipping threshold, increasing both the frequency and severity of gradient attenuation. This interaction motivates objective design that improves the conditioning of diffusion training before DP-SGD clipping. To address this problem, we develop a timestep-aware objective-conditioning method for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation trained with fixed-threshold DP-SGD. The method first adopts v v -prediction ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) as a target reparameterization to mitigate gradient amplification at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps. We then introduce static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control and, building on this control, develop diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting that applies stronger objective attenuation toward late low-SNR timesteps before clipping. The proposed method operates directly at the denoising-objective level while keeping the clipping-and-noise mechanism, sampling rule, and diffusion backbone fixed across objective variants. Recent studies have established the feasibility of training diffusion models with differential privacy across diverse generative and adaptation settings ( Dockhorn et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Tsai et al., 2025 ) . Building on this line of research, we investigate how denoising-objective design shapes pre-clipping gradient behavior and downstream imputation utility in energy time series. Experiments on five real-world energy time-series datasets evaluate the proposed method under matched DP-SGD settings. The engineering evaluation covers random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities. We further examine suffix-missing forecasting using the same conditional diffusion model, extending the evaluation to a forecasting setting. A controlled target–weighting decomposition separates the effects of target reparameterization and timestep-aware dynamic weighting, while additional matched DP-SGD settings assess the consistency of these trends across training conditions. Under the main matched DP-SGD setting, the proposed method improves imputation utility over the standard ε \varepsilon -prediction diffusion baseline. Gradient diagnostics further reveal lower high-percentile pre-clipping gradient norms and reduced overall clipping fractions, together with stronger gradient attenuation at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps. Our contributions are: 1. AI methodological contribution: Objective–clipping problem formulation and timestep-aware objective conditioning. We formulate the interaction between cosine-scheduled diffusion objectives and fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping as an objective-design problem in energy time-series imputation. We develop a timestep-aware objective-conditioning method that combines v v -prediction as target reparameterization, static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting to attenuate the objective more strongly at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps. 2. AI methodological contribution: Local characterization of gradient and clipping behavior. We characterize how deterministic timestep weighting changes pre-clipping gradient norms and the effective clipping boundary on the unweighted-gradient scale. A controlled target–weighting decomposition further separates the effects of target reparameterization and timestep-aware dynamic weighting under matched DP-SGD settings. 3. Engineering application contribution: Validation across real-world energy time series. We evaluate the proposed method on five real-world energy time-series datasets across random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, multiple missing-data severities, suffix-missing forecasting, and matched DP-SGD settings. The resulting utility improvements, together with gradient diagnostics, support the effectiveness of timestep-aware objective conditioning across multiple energy time-series recovery scenarios.

sections.heading: 2.1 Private Diffusion Optimization
sections.text: Differential privacy in deep learning is commonly implemented through differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD), which applies fixed-threshold gradient clipping before adding calibrated noise ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) . Because gradients exceeding the threshold are rescaled before noise addition, the distribution of pre-clipping gradient norms directly affects the optimization signal available during private training. Recent studies have extended diffusion models to differentially private training. DPDM investigates diffusion-model training under differential privacy ( Dockhorn et al., 2022 ) , DP-Promise improves private diffusion probabilistic models for image synthesis ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and DP-LoRA studies parameter-efficient private fine-tuning of diffusion models ( Tsai et al., 2025 ) . Collectively, these studies establish the feasibility of training diffusion models with differential privacy across diverse generative and adaptation settings, motivating further investigation of their optimization behavior under DP-SGD. The objective–clipping interaction at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps has received limited investigation in private diffusion training. Under cosine diffusion schedules ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ) , late diffusion timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where standard ε \varepsilon -prediction can produce large gradients before DP-SGD clipping. This motivates the investigation of objective conditioning for fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping, focusing on how denoising objectives shape pre-clipping gradient behavior and downstream utility.

sections.heading: 2.2 Objective Parameterization and Weighting
sections.text: Conditional diffusion models have been successfully applied to time-series imputation and interpolation, including CSDI, SSSD, and related masked-value reconstruction methods ( Tashiro et al., 2021 ; Alcaraz and Strodthoff, 2022 ; Cao et al., 2024 ) . These approaches establish diffusion modeling as an effective framework for reconstructing missing temporal observations and primarily focus on imputation quality, while their optimization behaviors under DP-SGD clipping are not explicitly characterized. In standard diffusion training, the denoising objective is commonly defined using ε \varepsilon -prediction ( Ho et al., 2020 ) . Alternative parameterizations such as v v -prediction can improve training stability and sample quality ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , while loss-weighting strategies such as Min-SNR weighting modify the relative contributions of diffusion timesteps in non-private training ( Hang et al., 2023 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) . These objective design strategies provide effective optimization mechanisms for diffusion models, while their effects on pre-clipping gradient behavior under fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping remain to be characterized. These findings motivate studying diffusion objective optimization under fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping. This perspective considers target reparameterization, static loss weighting, and timestep-aware dynamic weighting as objective components that shape pre-clipping gradient behavior and recovery utility under private training. Beyond diffusion-based approaches, representative time-series architectures such as PatchTST ( Nie et al., 2022 ) , TimesNet ( Wu et al., 2022 ) , and iTransformer ( Liu et al., 2023 ) have shown strong performance in forecasting and general time-series modeling. Following the comparison setting adopted in TimeDiT ( Cao et al., 2024 ) , these models provide non-diffusion references for evaluating time-series recovery performance.

sections.heading: 2.3 Energy Time-Series Interpolation and Privacy
sections.text: Energy monitoring systems provide an important application scenario for time-series imputation, where sensor faults, communication interruptions, device malfunctions, and signal-transmission problems can lead to missing measurements ( Lotfipoor et al., 2023 ) . Fine-grained energy records can also contain privacy-sensitive information: smart-meter measurements can reveal household activities ( Molina-Markham et al., 2010 ) , and residential electricity-consumption profiles can be used to infer occupancy patterns ( Razavi et al., 2019 ) . These studies establish accurate imputation and privacy-aware learning as important requirements in practical energy-data analysis. Recent diffusion-based approaches have improved energy-related time-series recovery by modeling complex temporal dependencies and conditional generation processes. Meanwhile, energy privacy studies have primarily focused on disclosure risks and privacy-preserving mechanisms. These directions demonstrate the importance of both recovery utility and privacy considerations in energy applications. However, the interaction between diffusion objective optimization and fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping in energy time-series recovery has received limited attention. Energy monitoring therefore provides a concrete engineering setting for studying how diffusion objective conditioning influences pre-clipping gradient behavior and recovery utility under private training. Overall, prior work establishes three closely related directions: differentially private diffusion training, diffusion objective design for time-series recovery, and energy time-series imputation with privacy considerations. Their intersection—how cosine-scheduled diffusion objectives shape pre-clipping gradient behavior under fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping and how this behavior relates to recovery utility—remains insufficiently characterized. This motivates the timestep-aware objective-conditioning method studied in this work.

sections.heading: Time-series interpolation under DP-SGD
sections.text: We consider diffusion-based time-series interpolation trained with DP-SGD. Let x 0 ∈ ℝ T × D x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D} denote a time-series segment, where T T is the temporal length and D D denotes the feature dimension. A binary mask m ∈ { 0 , 1 } T × D m\in\{0,1\}^{T\times D} indicates observed entries. The model is conditioned on c = ( x 0 ⊙ m , m ) , c=(x_{0}\odot m,m), and reconstructs the masked values ( 1 − m ) ⊙ x 0 (1-m)\odot x_{0} . The time series is segmented into non-overlapping windows, with each window treated as an independent training record for DP-SGD. The privacy unit is defined at the window level, and no cross-window record aggregation is performed. The resulting task is masked-value interpolation.

This timestep-dependent signal variation provides the basis for designing objective conditioning aligned with the diffusion process.

sections.heading: 3.2 Our Method: Timestep-Aware Objective Conditioning
sections.text: The denoising objective provides a mechanism for conditioning gradients before DP-SGD clipping. In the core objective comparisons, we keep the backbone, optimizer, masking protocol, clipping threshold, noise multiplier, and sampling protocol fixed across objective variants. The proposed timestep-aware objective-conditioning method modifies only the prediction target and timestep-dependent weighting.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: We evaluate the proposed timestep-aware objective-conditioning method for differentially private diffusion-based energy time-series interpolation. The task is masked-value interpolation: given partially observed inputs, the model reconstructs the masked values. We use five real-world energy time-series datasets: ETTh1 and ETTm1 ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) , Electricity ( Trindade, 2015 ) , Individual Household Electric Power Consumption ( Hebrail and Berard, 2012 ) , and Appliances Energy Prediction ( Candanedo et al., 2017 ) . For interpolation, we consider random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, and persistent outage missingness at missing ratios of 10 % 10\% , 20 % 20\% , 30 % 30\% , and 50 % 50\% . These patterns represent different structures of missing energy measurements, ranging from isolated measurement loss to temporary communication interruption and prolonged sensor or device unavailability. We additionally evaluate suffix-missing forecasting as an extended task setting. Based on the controlled target–weighting decomposition defined in Section 3.2 , we compare four objective variants: ε \varepsilon -prediction without weighting ( ε \varepsilon -pred.), ε \varepsilon -prediction with timestep-aware dynamic weighting ( ε \varepsilon -pred., dynamic), unweighted v v -prediction ( v v -pred., unweighted), and v v -prediction with timestep-aware dynamic weighting ( v v -pred., dynamic). Static loss weighting with λ ∈ { 0.6 , 0.9 } \lambda\in\{0.6,0.9\} is additionally used as a uniform-scaling control in the progressive objective ablation. Unless otherwise stated, the core objective variants and static loss weighting controls use the same DP-SGD protocol and share the same backbone, masking protocol, optimizer, training steps, sampling rule, clipping threshold, noise multiplier, and checkpoint selection rule. The main experiments are conducted under a matched DP-SGD setting with ( ϵ , δ ) = ( 10 , 10 − 5 ) (\epsilon,\delta)=(10,10^{-5}) . Sensitivity analyses further evaluate matched settings at ϵ ∈ { 6 , 8 } \epsilon\in\{6,8\} , while comparisons with external baselines additionally report results at ϵ = 8 \epsilon=8 alongside the main ϵ = 10 \epsilon=10 setting. All predictions are inverse-transformed using the same pre-specified normalization protocol before computing MSE, MAE, and RMSE. Within each dataset and evaluation condition, all methods are evaluated on the same data scale and target positions; interpolation metrics are computed only on masked positions, and forecasting metrics only over the forecast horizon. Unless otherwise stated, reported results are averaged over three random seeds ( 42 42 , 43 43 , and 44 44 ). Seed-level variability and additional implementation details are reported in the appendix. The experiments evaluate interpolation utility and mechanism-related gradient behavior at complementary levels. MSE, MAE, and RMSE quantify interpolation utility, while the controlled target–weighting decomposition separates target reparameterization from timestep-aware dynamic weighting. The controlled gradient diagnostic examines the timestep-dependent gradient attenuation characterized by Proposition 1 , while the training-time gradient diagnostics report high-percentile pre-clipping gradient norms and overall clipping fractions in relation to Proposition 2 and Corollary 1 .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We proposed a timestep-aware objective-conditioning method for differentially private diffusion-based energy time-series interpolation. The method addresses the objective–clipping interaction that becomes pronounced at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps, where standard ε \varepsilon -prediction can produce large gradients before DP-SGD clipping. Starting from ε \varepsilon -prediction, the objective is progressively reformulated through v v -prediction as target reparameterization, static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and timestep-aware dynamic weighting that applies stronger objective attenuation at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps while leaving the DP-SGD mechanism unchanged. The controlled decomposition of target reparameterization and weighting shows that target reparameterization is the primary source of the utility improvement, while timestep-aware dynamic weighting provides an additional gain under the main matched DP-SGD configuration. The gradient diagnostics further support the mechanism characterized in Section 3.3 . The controlled gradient diagnostic shows progressively stronger gradient attenuation toward late low-SNR diffusion timesteps, consistent with the scaling induced by deterministic timestep weighting, while the training-time gradient diagnostics show lower high-percentile pre-clipping gradient norms and a lower overall clipping fraction for the proposed method. Experiments on five real-world energy time-series datasets show that the proposed method improves over standard ε \varepsilon -prediction across random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, and persistent outage missingness under the main matched DP-SGD configuration. These improvements are also retained across the evaluated missing-data severities and in suffix-missing forecasting. Comparisons with representative time-series baselines and a validation-tuned ε \varepsilon -prediction baseline further demonstrate the robustness of the observed utility improvements under matched DP-SGD configurations. Overall, the results show that clipping-aware objective conditioning can improve both clipping behavior and interpolation utility under fixed-threshold DP-SGD, supporting practical energy time-series recovery under privacy constraints.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: The current evaluation uses a cosine diffusion schedule, a fixed diffusion backbone, and the matched DP-SGD configurations considered in this study. The incremental gain from timestep-aware dynamic weighting varies with the training configuration and task setting. Future evaluation should consider additional diffusion backbones and schedules, alternative private optimization settings, broader timestep-aware weighting strategies, and dedicated time-series imputation baselines. The current study adopts a window-level privacy unit, where non-overlapping windows are treated as independent training records.

sections.heading: Appendix B Implementation Details
sections.text: This appendix provides the implementation and training details used in the core objective comparisons. Within each dataset, the data are first split chronologically into 70 % / 10 % / 20 % 70\%/10\%/20\% training, validation, and test subsets. Dataset-specific missing-value processing is performed independently within each subset before normalization and window construction. Min–max normalization is applied per channel using statistics computed from the training subset only; the resulting parameters are fixed and reused for validation and test. The normalized series are then partitioned into non-overlapping fixed-length windows, each serving as an independent training record for DP-SGD. ETTh1, ETTm1, Household, and Appliances use a window length and stride of 96, whereas Electricity uses a window length and stride of 192. For Electricity, we retain the global one-channel construction and use MT_369 as the fixed evaluation sensor. For Household, the target variable is Global_active_power , retained at the original one-minute resolution. After the chronological split, interior missing values are linearly interpolated independently within each subset, while leading and trailing missing values are removed. Linearly interpolated values are excluded from the evaluation targets. For Appliances, we use Appliances at the original ten-minute resolution. No additional resampling is applied to Household or Appliances. The diffusion backbone is a DiT-style Transformer conditioned through AdaLN-Zero. Its architectural configuration is summarized in Table 10 . The same backbone, optimizer, training masking protocol, and diffusion training configuration are used across all core objective variants. The controlled comparisons differ only in the prediction target and/or loss weighting. For each training run, checkpoint selection follows the same validation-based rule, and the checkpoint with the best validation performance is used for evaluation. Predictions are inverse-transformed using the fixed training-derived normalization parameters before computing MSE, MAE, and RMSE. Within each dataset and evaluation condition, all compared objective variants use the same data scale, target positions, and evaluation protocol. For interpolation, random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, and persistent outage missingness are applied at evaluation time with missing ratios of 10 % 10\% , 20 % 20\% , 30 % 30\% , and 50 % 50\% . Artificial missingness is applied only to originally observed positions, and interpolation metrics are computed only over the resulting masked targets. Suffix-missing forecasting uses the same interpolation-trained checkpoints, with the final H ∈ { 24 , 48 , 72 } H\in\{24,48,72\} positions treated as the prediction target and metrics computed only over the forecast horizon. No separate forecasting architecture or forecasting-specific training objective is introduced. For each evaluation condition, 30 diffusion samples are generated using DDIM with 50 inference steps. sections.heading: Appendix I Controlled Gradient Diagnostic
sections.text: The training-time gradient diagnostics in Section 4.3.3 characterize the gradient distributions for individual private examples encountered during actual DP-SGD optimization. Because those diagnostics are obtained from separately trained objective variants, they do not isolate the immediate effect of timestep-aware dynamic weighting at a fixed model state. We therefore conduct an additional controlled gradient diagnostic in which the model state and stochastic inputs are matched and only the weighting rule is changed from λ t = 1 \lambda_{t}=1 to λ t = α ¯ t \lambda_{t}=\bar{\alpha}_{t} .

sections.heading: I.1 Diagnostic Setup
sections.text: We fix a trained v v -prediction checkpoint and keep the model state, input batch, observation mask, diffusion noise, and timestep realizations identical between two objective evaluations. No parameter update is performed during the diagnostic. Let G u G_{u} and G d G_{d} denote the pre-clipping aggregate gradients formed from the corresponding unclipped gradients for the private examples under the unweighted and dynamically weighted objectives, respectively. In the present setting, different examples are associated with different sampled diffusion timesteps and therefore receive different values of λ t \lambda_{t} . Because both evaluations use the same v v -prediction target, this diagnostic isolates the effect of timestep-aware dynamic weighting rather than target reparameterization. In DP-SGD, clipping is applied to the gradient for each private example before aggregation; accordingly, the pre-clipping aggregate-gradient norms in this diagnostic are not used to define clipping events or overall clipping fractions.

sections.heading: I.4 Relation to Training-Time Gradient Diagnostics
sections.text: The controlled gradient diagnostic and the training-time gradient diagnostics capture complementary aspects of the optimization process. Section 4.3.3 characterizes the gradient distribution for individual private examples encountered during actual DP-SGD training, whereas the controlled gradient diagnostic isolates the immediate effect of timestep-aware dynamic weighting at a fixed model state. The mixed-timestep results show that timestep-aware dynamic weighting changes the relative contributions to the pre-clipping aggregate gradient, while the timestep-stratified results show that this effect becomes more pronounced toward late low-SNR diffusion timesteps. These observations are consistent with the training-time gradient diagnostics and with the illustrative timestep-wise gradient diagnostic in Figure 2 , and provide additional empirical support for the theoretical mechanism characterized in Section 3.3 .

Diffusion models trained with differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) provide a promising framework for privacy-sensitive energy time-series imputation. Under cosine diffusion schedules, late timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where standard ε \varepsilon -prediction can induce large pre-clipping gradients. Such gradients are more likely to be clipped, reducing the retained optimization signal. The artificial intelligence (AI) contribution lies in formulating this objective–clipping interaction as an objective optimization problem under fixed-threshold DP-SGD and developing timestep-aware objective conditioning for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation. The method adopts v v -prediction to mitigate late-timestep gradient amplification, uses static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and introduces diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting for stronger attenuation before clipping. For the engineering application, we evaluate the method on five real-world energy time-series datasets across random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities. Under matched DP-SGD settings, the proposed method consistently improves imputation utility over the ε \varepsilon -prediction baseline. Gradient diagnostics reveal lower upper-tail pre-clipping gradient norms, reduced clipping fractions, and stronger attenuation at late low-SNR timesteps, supporting the effectiveness of clipping-aware objective conditioning for energy time-series imputation. Keywords: Diffusion models , Time-series imputation , Energy time series , Differential privacy , Gradient clipping , Objective conditioning 1 Introduction Time-series data in energy monitoring systems often contain missing observations because of sensor faults, communication interruptions, device malfunctions, and signal transmission problems ( Lotfipoor et al., 2023 ) . In applications such as transformer monitoring, smart metering, electricity-load monitoring, and building energy management, imputation is needed to recover missing measurements, while the underlying temporal records may contain sensitive personal or operational information. In particular, fine-grained household electricity-consumption profiles can reveal household activities and occupancy patterns ( Molina-Markham et al., 2010 ; Razavi et al., 2019 ) . Differential privacy therefore provides a principled training framework for energy time-series imputation involving sensitive measurements ( Dwork and Roth, 2014 ; Mao et al., 2024 ) . Diffusion models are particularly well suited to this task because they learn conditional denoising processes for reconstructing missing values ( Tashiro et al., 2021 ; Alcaraz and Strodthoff, 2022 ; Cao et al., 2024 ) . However, under differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD), the denoising objective directly interacts with fixed-threshold gradient clipping. When the objective induces large per-example gradients, clipping attenuates their contributions to the optimization update and can degrade training utility ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) . We identify an objective–clipping interaction that becomes pronounced at late diffusion timesteps, where diffusion timesteps are distinct from training iterations. Under cosine schedules, late diffusion timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ) . In this regime, standard ε \varepsilon -prediction can induce large pre-clipping gradients that exceed the fixed clipping threshold, increasing both the frequency and severity of gradient attenuation. This interaction motivates objective design that improves the conditioning of diffusion training before DP-SGD clipping. To address this problem, we develop a timestep-aware objective-conditioning method for diffusion-based energy time-series imputation trained with fixed-threshold DP-SGD. The method first adopts v v -prediction ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) as a target reparameterization to mitigate gradient amplification at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps. We then introduce static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control and, building on this control, develop diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting that applies stronger objective attenuation toward late low-SNR timesteps before clipping. The proposed method operates directly at the denoising-objective level while keeping the clipping-and-noise mechanism, sampling rule, and diffusion backbone fixed across objective variants. Recent studies have established the feasibility of training diffusion models with differential privacy across diverse generative and adaptation settings ( Dockhorn et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Tsai et al., 2025 ) . Building on this line of research, we investigate how denoising-objective design shapes pre-clipping gradient behavior and downstream imputation utility in energy time series. Experiments on five real-world energy time-series datasets evaluate the proposed method under matched DP-SGD settings. The engineering evaluation covers random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, and multiple missing-data severities. We further examine suffix-missing forecasting using the same conditional diffusion model, extending the evaluation to a forecasting setting. A controlled target–weighting decomposition separates the effects of target reparameterization and timestep-aware dynamic weighting, while additional matched DP-SGD settings assess the consistency of these trends across training conditions. Under the main matched DP-SGD setting, the proposed method improves imputation utility over the standard ε \varepsilon -prediction diffusion baseline. Gradient diagnostics further reveal lower high-percentile pre-clipping gradient norms and reduced overall clipping fractions, together with stronger gradient attenuation at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps. Our contributions are: 1. AI methodological contribution: Objective–clipping problem formulation and timestep-aware objective conditioning. We formulate the interaction between cosine-scheduled diffusion objectives and fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping as an objective-design problem in energy time-series imputation. We develop a timestep-aware objective-conditioning method that combines v v -prediction as target reparameterization, static loss weighting as a uniform-scaling control, and diffusion-schedule-aware dynamic weighting to attenuate the objective more strongly at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps. 2. AI methodological contribution: Local characterization of gradient and clipping behavior. We characterize how deterministic timestep weighting changes pre-clipping gradient norms and the effective clipping boundary on the unweighted-gradient scale. A controlled target–weighting decomposition further separates the effects of target reparameterization and timestep-aware dynamic weighting under matched DP-SGD settings. 3. Engineering application contribution: Validation across real-world energy time series. We evaluate the proposed method on five real-world energy time-series datasets across random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, persistent outages, multiple missing-data severities, suffix-missing forecasting, and matched DP-SGD settings. The resulting utility improvements, together with gradient diagnostics, support the effectiveness of timestep-aware objective conditioning across multiple energy time-series recovery scenarios. 2 Related Work 2.1 Private Diffusion Optimization Differential privacy in deep learning is commonly implemented through differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD), which applies fixed-threshold gradient clipping before adding calibrated noise ( Abadi et al., 2016 ) . Because gradients exceeding the threshold are rescaled before noise addition, the distribution of pre-clipping gradient norms directly affects the optimization signal available during private training. Recent studies have extended diffusion models to differentially private training. DPDM investigates diffusion-model training under differential privacy ( Dockhorn et al., 2022 ) , DP-Promise improves private diffusion probabilistic models for image synthesis ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and DP-LoRA studies parameter-efficient private fine-tuning of diffusion models ( Tsai et al., 2025 ) . Collectively, these studies establish the feasibility of training diffusion models with differential privacy across diverse generative and adaptation settings, motivating further investigation of their optimization behavior under DP-SGD. The objective–clipping interaction at late low-SNR diffusion timesteps has received limited investigation in private diffusion training. Under cosine diffusion schedules ( Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021 ) , late diffusion timesteps correspond to low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions, where standard ε \varepsilon -prediction can produce large gradients before DP-SGD clipping. This motivates the investigation of objective conditioning for fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping, focusing on how denoising objectives shape pre-clipping gradient behavior and downstream utility. 2.2 Objective Parameterization and Weighting Conditional diffusion models have been successfully applied to time-series imputation and interpolation, including CSDI, SSSD, and related masked-value reconstruction methods ( Tashiro et al., 2021 ; Alcaraz and Strodthoff, 2022 ; Cao et al., 2024 ) . These approaches establish diffusion modeling as an effective framework for reconstructing missing temporal observations and primarily focus on imputation quality, while their optimization behaviors under DP-SGD clipping are not explicitly characterized. In standard diffusion training, the denoising objective is commonly defined using ε \varepsilon -prediction ( Ho et al., 2020 ) . Alternative parameterizations such as v v -prediction can improve training stability and sample quality ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , while loss-weighting strategies such as Min-SNR weighting modify the relative contributions of diffusion timesteps in non-private training ( Hang et al., 2023 ; Karras et al., 2022 ) . These objective design strategies provide effective optimization mechanisms for diffusion models, while their effects on pre-clipping gradient behavior under fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping remain to be characterized. These findings motivate studying diffusion objective optimization under fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping. This perspective considers target reparameterization, static loss weighting, and timestep-aware dynamic weighting as objective components that shape pre-clipping gradient behavior and recovery utility under private training. Beyond diffusion-based approaches, representative time-series architectures such as PatchTST ( Nie et al., 2022 ) , TimesNet ( Wu et al., 2022 ) , and iTransformer ( Liu et al., 2023 ) have shown strong performance in forecasting and general time-series modeling. Following the comparison setting adopted in TimeDiT ( Cao et al., 2024 ) , these models provide non-diffusion references for evaluating time-series recovery performance. 2.3 Energy Time-Series Interpolation and Privacy Energy monitoring systems provide an important application scenario for time-series imputation, where sensor faults, communication interruptions, device malfunctions, and signal-transmission problems can lead to missing measurements ( Lotfipoor et al., 2023 ) . Fine-grained energy records can also contain privacy-sensitive information: smart-meter measurements can reveal household activities ( Molina-Markham et al., 2010 ) , and residential electricity-consumption profiles can be used to infer occupancy patterns ( Razavi et al., 2019 ) . These studies establish accurate imputation and privacy-aware learning as important requirements in practical energy-data analysis. Recent diffusion-based approaches have improved energy-related time-series recovery by modeling complex temporal dependencies and conditional generation processes. Meanwhile, energy privacy studies have primarily focused on disclosure risks and privacy-preserving mechanisms. These directions demonstrate the importance of both recovery utility and privacy considerations in energy applications. However, the interaction between diffusion objective optimization and fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping in energy time-series recovery has received limited attention. Energy monitoring therefore provides a concrete engineering setting for studying how diffusion objective conditioning influences pre-clipping gradient behavior and recovery utility under private training. Overall, prior work establishes three closely related directions: differentially private diffusion training, diffusion objective design for time-series recovery, and energy time-series imputation with privacy considerations. Their intersection—how cosine-scheduled diffusion objectives shape pre-clipping gradient behavior under fixed-threshold DP-SGD clipping and how this behavior relates to recovery utility—remains insufficiently characterized. This motivates the timestep-aware objective-conditioning method studied in this work. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries Time-series interpolation under DP-SGD We consider diffusion-based time-series interpolation trained with DP-SGD. The task is masked-value interpolation: given partially observed inputs, the model reconstructs the masked values. We use five real-world energy time-series datasets: ETTh1 and ETTm1 ( Zhou et al., 2021 ) , Electricity ( Trindade, 2015 ) , Individual Household Electric Power Consumption ( Hebrail and Berard, 2012 ) , and Appliances Energy Prediction ( Candanedo et al., 2017 ) . For interpolation, we consider random point missingness, contiguous block missingness, and persistent outage missingness at missing ratios of 10 % 10\% , 20 % 20\% , 30 % 30\% , and 50 % 50\% . These patterns represent different structures of missing energy measurements, ranging from isolated measurement loss to temporary communication interruption and prolonged sensor or device unavailability. We additionally evaluate suffix-missing forecasting as an extended task setting. Based on the controlled target–weighting decomposition defined in Section 3.2 , we compare four objective variants: ε \varepsilon -prediction without weighting ( ε \varepsilon -pred.), ε \varepsilon -prediction with timestep-aware dynamic weighting ( ε \varepsilon -pred., dynamic), unweighted v v -prediction ( v v -pred., unweighted), and v v -prediction with timestep-aware dynamic weighting ( v v -pred., dynamic). Static loss weighting with λ ∈ { 0.6 , 0.9 } \lambda\in\{0.6,0.9\} is additionally used as a uniform-scaling control in the progressive objective ablation. Unless otherwise stated, the core objective variants and static loss weighting controls use the same DP-SGD protocol and share the same backbone, masking protocol, optimizer, training steps, sampling rule, clipping threshold, noise multiplier, and checkpoint selection rule. The main experiments are conducted under a matched DP-SGD setting with ( ϵ , δ ) = ( 10 , 10 − 5 ) (\epsilon,\delta)=(10,10^{-5}) . Sensitivity analyses further evaluate matched settings at ϵ ∈ { 6 , 8 } \epsilon\in\{6,8\} , while comparisons with external baselines additionally report results at ϵ = 8 \epsilon=8 alongside the main ϵ = 10 \epsilon=10 setting. All predictions are inverse-transformed using the same pre-specified normalization protocol before computing MSE, MAE, and RMSE. Within each dataset and evaluation condition, all methods are evaluated on the same data scale and target positions; interpolation metrics are computed only on masked positions, and forecasting metrics only over the forecast horizon. Unless otherwise stated, reported results are averaged over three random seeds ( 42 42 , 43 43 , and 44 44 ). Seed-level variability and additional implementation details are reported in the appendix. The experiments evaluate interpolation utility and mechanism-related gradient behavior at complementary levels. MSE, MAE, and RMSE quantify interpolation utility, while the controlled target–weighting decomposition separates target reparameterization from timestep-aware dynamic weighting.
